plan_turns.user: Ok so the plan says I can count on $41,000 a year, and I'm wondering what happens if I push out the retirement date a bit. Like if I keep working till 65 instead of 62, does the boat still fit? I've been eyeing a bigger one, a 28 footer, but that's a whole other story with my buddy Ray and the marina fees.
plan_turns.text: From the source: "Generally, when you turn 65. This is called your Initial Enrollment Period. It lasts for 7 months, starting 3 months before you turn 65, and ending 3 months after the month you turn 65."

plan_turns.user: So that Medicare thing is about health insurance, right? Anyway, my question was about the boat. If I work till 65 instead of 62, does the plan still work? Ray says I'm crazy for keeping the 22 footer, but a 28 footer at the marina runs real money every year, and I want to know if I can swing it at 62 or whether I'm stuck working longer.
plan_turns.text: From the source: "Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 and 63 who participate in these plans. For 2027, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $11,750 instead of the $8,500 noted above."

plan_turns.user: Huh, okay, that's a lot of numbers about catch-up stuff, and I'm not sure what it has to do with my boat. Ray's at the marina every Saturday telling me the 28 footer is the only real boat, so I'm trying to figure out if I can actually afford it. Can you tell me what the plan says my savings look like if I quit at 62 versus 65? Just the total, I can't keep track of all these percentages.
plan_turns.text: The plan does not give a separate savings total for retiring at 62 versus 65, so I cannot give you those two totals. What I can say: you have about $535,000 saved now, and the plan's median projection at retirement (age 62) is about $640,000. The plan says your spending goal of about $56,100 a year is below what your savings are expected to cover, so the plan's verdict is "below goal." Ask a licensed adviser to run the age 65 numbers before you decide on the boat.

plan_turns.user: Okay so below goal, that's not great but not a disaster either, right? Ray would say the same thing, he's always got an opinion on the money. My question now is more practical. If I do end up buying the 28 footer, what should I do first, sell the 22 or just run the numbers on the bigger slip fee? I've got about 70 grand in the regular brokerage account and the rest is in the 401k, so I don't know which one I'd pull from.
plan_turns.text: From the source: "If you start receiving benefits early, your benefits will be reduced a small percentage for each month before your full retirement age"

plan_turns.user: Huh, that's about Social Security reductions, which I'm not sure applies to me yet. Look, before I get into the boat question, what does the plan actually assume about me? Like what age it thinks I'm retiring at, how much I spend, and what it's counting on from the house. Ray's always saying these planners use made-up numbers, and I'd like to see what they're working from.
plan_turns.text: The plan assumes you retire at 62, which is 7 years from now, and it plans to age 93. It assumes you spend about $78,000 a year now, or $6,500 a month. Your spending goal in retirement is $56,100 a year, or $4,675 a month. Of that, $41,000 a year is the safe amount the plan expects your savings to cover, and the plan counts on $37,000 a year from Social Security starting at age 70. The house matters because the mortgage ends in 2030, which the plan expects to cut your yearly costs by $7,900. The plan does not count on any home sale or home equity. Under these figures, the plan shows you below your goal.
